extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and researchers interested in the history and selection practices of The Best American Short Stories anthology series
extracted.subtask_description: A summary of the editorial standards, historical preferences, and procedural selection rules used by The Best American Short Stories series (1915–present). Covers early editors' literary standards, mid-century tastes, and the post-1978 series/guest-editor selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Brien's three-star ranking (literary permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edward O'Brien's editions contained lengthy tabulations of stories and magazines, ranked on a scale of three stars (representing O'Brien's notion of their 'literary permanence'). He claimed to read around 8,000 stories a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as an explicit evaluative metric used by the early series editor to indicate perceived lasting literary value; implies prioritizing 'literary permanence' when selecting stories. Example/annotation: large-scale reading and tabulation of magazine stories to rank them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciously literary development; avoid formulaic/sentimental commercial fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Brien was deeply and vocally skeptical of the value of commercial short fiction, which he said tended to the formulaic and sentimental; he insisted on the need for a consciously literary development of the short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favored stories that demonstrated literary ambition, experimentation, and higher standards rather than formulaic plots or sentimentalism. Anti-pattern: choosing stories primarily for commercial appeal or formulaic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foley-era preference for sharply observed, realistic stories that eschew trite conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Martha Foley the series tended toward sharply observed, generally realistic stories that eschewed trite conventions, while also attending to new currents in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favors close observation, realism, and avoidance of cliché; evidence in selections of authors like John Cheever and Bernard Malamud. Also includes openness to emerging styles (e.g., Donald Barthelme) and some attention to minority literature, though the series may have been uneven in perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-1978 formal selection procedure: series editor recommends 120; guest editor selects 20
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1978 the series editor recommends 120 stories each year; a different guest editor of reputation then selects the best twenty stories from that recommended pool and writes the volume introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement and implicit quality filter: being among the 120 recommended is a threshold for consideration; final selection is subjective to guest editor's judgment. Note: guest editors have occasionally gone beyond the series editor's recommendations (example: John Gardner in 1982).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest editor must be a writer of reputation and may exercise discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The series format since 1978 designated a different writer of reputation to select the contents and introduce the volume each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial standard that selections reflect the taste and judgment of a prominent writer; allows for individual editorial voice and discretion, including diverging from the series editor's recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to minority literature and new currents (as a selection consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The series (notably under Foley) at times attended to the rise of minority literature and new currents in fiction (e.g., dedicating a volume to Leslie Marmon Silko; choice of Donald Barthelme in 1976).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection can include works that represent emergent or underrepresented literary voices; the page notes the series was sometimes less perceptive in this area, signaling a criterion of cultural and stylistic awareness but also historical unevenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selections as a running judgement of contemporary tastes / historical context matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics have observed that individual volumes provide a running judgement of tastes regarding short stories across the decades — they reflect the stories judges in each era chose, offering a sense of how writers and tastes have changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit evaluative dimension: when assessing inclusion, consider how selections align with contemporary critical tastes and historical context. The anthology's value includes its role as a historical record of changing judgments rather than a single absolute standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary source pool: stories originally published in popular magazines and periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: The most popular magazines of the early 20th century featured short fiction prominently; selections historically drew from magazine-published stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical sourcing criterion: stories' original magazine publication was the typical pool for consideration. Editors historically read many magazines (O'Brien claimed ~8,000 stories/year), so visibility in prominent periodicals increased chances of being noticed.
